articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $2.1M tourism contract renewed without competitive bid
articles.dek: The Tourist Development Council quietly extended its marketing agreement with a Tallahassee firm last week. Three commissioners say they weren't briefed on alternatives.
brief: Escambia County's Tourist Development Council approved a $2.1 million contract extension with Tallahassee-based Visit Florida Partners without issuing a competitive bid
Three county commissioners say they received no briefing on alternative marketing firms before the TDC voted to renew the agreement
The contract, funded entirely by bed tax revenue, has been held by the same firm since 2019
articles.body:
The conference room on the third floor of the Escambia County Central Office Complex seats maybe forty people. Last Tuesday morning, nine showed up. Five were Tourist Development Council members. Two were county staff. The other two were representatives from Visit Florida Partners, the Tallahassee marketing firm that has handled Escambia County's tourism promotion for seven years.

The meeting lasted twenty-two minutes. In that time, the TDC voted 4-1 to extend the firm's contract for another three years at $700,000 annually. No other firms were considered. No request for proposals was issued. No presentation compared Visit Florida Partners' performance against industry benchmarks or competing agencies.

The lone dissenting vote came from TDC member Patricia Harmon, a Gulf Breeze hotelier who has served on the council since 2021.

"I asked a simple question," Harmon said in an interview Friday. "What else is out there? Nobody had an answer. Or nobody wanted to give one."

How the contract works

The Tourist Development Council is an advisory body that recommends how Escambia County should spend revenue from its 5% bed tax—the fee added to hotel and short-term rental stays. In fiscal year 2025, that tax generated $14.2 million. The TDC allocates those funds across beach renourishment, sports tourism, special events and destination marketing.

The marketing contract with Visit Florida Partners represents the single largest discretionary expenditure the TDC controls. The firm handles digital advertising, travel media relations, seasonal campaigns and the visitpensacola.com website.

Under Florida law, contracts of this size typically require competitive bidding. But tourism marketing agreements can qualify for an exemption if the service is deemed "professional" in nature—a category that includes advertising and public relations.

Escambia County Attorney Alison Rogers confirmed the exemption applies here. "The county has discretion," Rogers said. "Competitive bidding is encouraged but not mandated for professional services contracts."

The county last issued an RFP for tourism marketing in 2019. Visit Florida Partners won that bid against two other firms. Since then, the contract has been renewed twice without reopening the process.

Commissioners say they were left out

The TDC is advisory. Final spending authority rests with the five-member Escambia County Board of County Commissioners. But commissioners typically defer to TDC recommendations on tourism matters, and the contract renewal was placed on the commission's consent agenda—a batch of routine items approved without individual discussion.

Commissioner Doug Underhill voted to approve the consent agenda at last Thursday's commission meeting. He said he didn't realize the tourism contract was included until a constituent emailed him afterward.

"That's on me," Underhill said. "But it's also on staff. A $2.1 million commitment should come with a briefing. I got nothing."

Commissioners Lumon May and Steven Barry echoed Underhill's concern. May said he assumed the TDC had vetted alternatives. Barry said he would have requested a presentation had he known the contract was up for renewal.

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, who serves as the commission's liaison to the TDC, defended the process. "Visit Florida Partners has delivered," Bergosh said. "Our tourism numbers are up. Our brand visibility is up. Why would we blow that up to chase some hypothetical better deal?"

Performance questions

Visit Florida Partners' contract includes annual performance metrics tied to website traffic, advertising impressions and earned media placements. According to a summary provided to the TDC, the firm met or exceeded all benchmarks in 2025.

But those benchmarks were set by the firm itself, based on projections it submitted when the contract was last renewed in 2023. The county does not independently audit the metrics or compare them to peer destinations.

Harmon, the dissenting TDC member, said that's the core problem. "We're grading their homework with their own answer key," she said. "I'm not saying they're doing a bad job. I'm saying I genuinely don't know, and neither does anyone else in that room."

A 2024 study by the Florida TaxWatch research institute found that Escambia County's tourism marketing spending per visitor ranks in the top third among Florida's 67 counties. But its visitor growth rate over the past five years falls in the bottom half.

Visit Florida Partners did not respond to requests for comment.

What happens next

The renewed contract takes effect October 1. Commissioners could theoretically rescind their approval at a future meeting, but none indicated plans to do so.

Underhill said he intends to request a full performance audit before the next renewal cycle. "Three years from now, I want numbers I can trust," he said. "And I want to see what other firms would charge for the same work."

Harmon said she'll push for the TDC to adopt a policy requiring competitive bids for any contract over $500,000, regardless of professional services exemptions.

"The bed tax isn't the county's money," Harmon said. "It's the tourists' money. It's the hotels' money. The least we can do is prove we're spending it wisely."

The next TDC meeting is scheduled for July 15.

articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Six months after the Bayou Texar dredging promise, residents still wait
articles.dek: The city allocated funds in January to address flooding and navigation issues. Permits remain pending, and some homeowners say they've stopped asking for updates.
brief: Pensacola City Council approved $2.1 million for Bayou Texar dredging in January, but permits from state and federal agencies remain pending six months later.
Sediment buildup has reduced navigable depth in portions of the bayou to less than two feet at low tide, stranding boats and worsening stormwater drainage.
City officials cite a backlog at the Florida Department of Environmental Protection, while residents say communication has been inconsistent at best.
articles.body:
The dock behind Marcus Webb's home on Bayou Texar used to accommodate a 22-foot bay boat. Now it holds a kayak.

"I gave up," Webb said, standing on the weathered planks one morning last week. The water beneath him was the color of sweet tea, maybe eighteen inches deep. "I sold the boat in March. Couldn't get it out half the time anyway."

Webb is one of roughly 200 property owners along Bayou Texar who have watched sediment accumulate for years, transforming a navigable urban waterway into something closer to a mud flat. In January, Pensacola City Council voted unanimously to allocate $2.1 million for dredging operations, a decision met with applause from the dozen residents who'd shown up to speak during public comment.

Six months later, not a single cubic yard of sediment has been removed.

Permits in purgatory

The holdup, according to city officials, is regulatory. Dredging projects in Florida require permits from multiple agencies: the Florida Department of Environmental Protection, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and potentially the Environmental Protection Agency if the sediment contains contaminants requiring special disposal.

Pensacola submitted its FDEP application in February. As of last week, it remained under review.

"We're in the queue," said Daniel Quimby, Pensacola's stormwater management director, during a phone interview. "FDEP has a significant backlog. We've been told to expect a decision by late summer, but that's not a guarantee."

The Corps of Engineers application, which the city filed in March, requires the FDEP permit as a precondition. That means any delay at the state level cascades forward.

Quimby said the city has followed up with FDEP monthly. He characterized the communication as "professional but not particularly informative."

FDEP spokesperson Mariana Castillo, in an emailed statement, confirmed the application was under review but declined to provide a timeline. "Each application is evaluated based on its specific environmental considerations," she wrote. "We do not comment on pending permits."

A bayou in decline

Bayou Texar runs roughly three miles from its headwaters near 12th Avenue to its confluence with Pensacola Bay. For decades it served as a recreational corridor—bass fishing, crabbing, small boat access to the bay. Homes along its banks command premium prices, or did.

The sedimentation problem isn't new. A 2019 city study found that portions of the bayou had lost more than four feet of depth since the 1980s, the result of stormwater runoff carrying soil from construction sites, eroding banks, and aging infrastructure. The study recommended dredging as the only viable long-term solution.

That recommendation sat untouched through the pandemic, through two budget cycles, through a mayoral transition. It wasn't until a series of flooding events in late 2025—when homes on the bayou's north shore took on water during a relatively modest rain event—that council members moved the project to the front of the line.

"This should have happened five years ago," said Pensacola City Council member Allison Patton, whose district includes much of the bayou. "We're paying for that delay now, both in dollars and in trust."

Communication breakdown

Residents say the January vote felt like a turning point. Several described attending the council meeting, shaking hands with officials afterward, exchanging phone numbers.

Then the updates stopped.

"I called the stormwater office in March, got a callback saying they were waiting on permits," said Linda Okonkwo, who has lived on the bayou for eleven years. "Called again in April. Same answer. I stopped calling."

Okonkwo said she understands that permitting takes time. What frustrates her is the absence of proactive communication. No email updates. No community meetings. No timeline posted on the city website.

"We're not children," she said. "Tell us it's going to be eighteen months. Tell us there's a problem. Just tell us something."

Quimby acknowledged that outreach has been limited. "Honestly, we didn't want to communicate uncertainty," he said. "We thought we'd have better news by now."

He said the city is planning a community meeting for late July, though no date has been set.

Money sitting idle

The $2.1 million allocated in January remains unspent, parked in a restricted fund. Under city rules, those dollars can't be redirected to other projects without council approval. They also can't earn meaningful interest sitting in a municipal account.

Meanwhile, construction costs continue to rise. Quimby said the city's original contractor bid, submitted in December 2025, included a price escalation clause that kicks in after nine months. If dredging doesn't begin by September, the project could cost an additional $180,000 to $250,000.

"We're aware of the clock," Quimby said. "We're doing everything we can to move this forward."

Council member Patton said she's asked the city attorney to explore whether Pensacola can begin any preliminary work—surveying, equipment staging—before the permits are finalized. The answer, so far, has been no.

"The regulatory framework exists for good reasons," Patton said. "But it wasn't designed for situations where everyone agrees the work needs to happen. There's no fast lane."

What comes next

Assuming FDEP issues its permit by August, and the Corps follows within sixty days, dredging could theoretically begin in late October. The work itself would take an estimated four to six months, meaning the bayou might not see full restoration until spring 2027—more than two years after the flooding that prompted the council vote.

That timeline assumes no complications: no contaminated sediment requiring special handling, no challenges from environmental groups, no hurricane disruptions during the fall season.

Webb, the homeowner who sold his boat, said he's not counting on any of it.

"I've lived here long enough to know how these things go," he said. "Something else will come up. Some other emergency. Some other priority."

He looked out at the bayou, where a great blue heron stood motionless in the shallows, unbothered by the depth.

"At least somebody can use it," Webb said.

articles.label: Community
articles.headline: Blue Angels practice crowds are back—and so are the parking wars on Pensacola Beach
articles.dek: Wednesday rehearsals draw thousands to the shore. Local businesses love it. Residents who can't reach their driveways have a different view.
brief: Blue Angels Wednesday practice sessions draw an estimated 8,000-12,000 spectators to Pensacola Beach each week during air show season
Casino Beach parking fills by 10 a.m. on practice days, pushing overflow vehicles into residential areas along Via de Luna and Ariola Drive
Escambia County is considering permit-only parking zones for beach residents after complaints doubled from last season
articles.body:
The F/A-18 Super Hornets hadn't even started their engines Wednesday morning when Linda Odom found a white Chevy Tahoe with Texas plates blocking her driveway on Ariola Drive.

She left a note on the windshield. Polite but firm. By the time the jets screamed overhead at 11:30 a.m., the Tahoe was gone. In its place sat a silver minivan from Alabama.

"This happens every single Wednesday from March through November," Odom said. "I love the Blues. I've lived here 18 years. But I can't get to my own house."

The Blue Angels practice schedule is no secret. Every Wednesday and most Tuesdays during the air show season, the Navy's flight demonstration squadron rehearses over Pensacola Beach. The sessions are free, spectacular, and draw crowds that rival small-town football games.

Escambia County estimates 8,000 to 12,000 people show up on a typical Wednesday. On clear days with light winds, those numbers climb higher.

The spectacle is good for business. The problem is where everyone parks.

Casino Beach fills fast

The main public lot at Casino Beach holds roughly 500 vehicles. It fills by 10 a.m. on practice days. Often earlier.

The overflow pushes east and west along Via de Luna Drive, the two-lane road that serves as Pensacola Beach's main artery. Visitors line the shoulders. They park on sandy patches between dunes. They squeeze into the driveways of rental properties whose owners aren't home.

Some walk a mile or more to the beach. Others give up and watch from their cars, engines running, air conditioning blasting against the June heat.

"We had a family set up lawn chairs in our front yard last month," said Tom Brennan, who owns a house on Panferio Drive. "Nice people. Asked if they could use our bathroom. But it's still strange."

The Santa Rosa Island Authority, which manages public beach access, has tried to spread the crowds. Signs direct visitors to Quietwater Beach on the sound side. Trolley service runs from the Pensacola Beach Boardwalk. Neither solution has put a dent in the parking crunch at Casino Beach, where spectators claim the best views of the team's maneuvers.

Complaints have doubled

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh said his office received 47 parking-related complaints tied to Blue Angels practices in 2025. This year, through the end of June, the count stands at 58.

"We're on pace to more than double last year," Bergosh said. "And summer just started."

The complaints range from blocked driveways to vehicles parked on private property to fire lane violations. The Escambia County Sheriff's Office has issued 112 parking citations on Pensacola Beach so far this season. Deputies towed nine vehicles in May alone.

Bergosh has proposed a permit-only parking zone for residents on several streets closest to Casino Beach. The idea mirrors systems used in beach towns across Florida. Homeowners would receive free passes. Everyone else would need to park elsewhere.

The proposal is scheduled for a county commission workshop in August. Bergosh said he expects pushback from visitors who've come to expect free parking anywhere they can find it.

"People don't like being told they can't park somewhere," he said. "But residents have rights too."

A Wednesday blessing

Not everyone on the beach sees the crowds as a curse.

At Flounder's Chowder House, general manager Kevin Satterfield said Wednesday lunch service during Blue Angels season outperforms Friday nights.

"We staff up like it's a holiday," Satterfield said. "People come early, they stay for the show, they eat, they drink. It's the best day of the week."

The Pensacola Beach Visitors Information Center reported a 23% increase in foot traffic on practice Wednesdays compared to the same days in non-practice weeks. Gift shops, ice cream stands, and beach rental outfits all see the bump.

For vacation rental owners, the practice schedule is a selling point. Listings on Airbnb and VRBO advertise "Blue Angels view" as a premium feature. Some properties charge $50 to $100 more per night during air show season.

"We book out months in advance for those weeks," said rental manager Diane Foley, who handles 14 properties on the beach. "People plan their whole vacation around the practice days."

The view from above

The Blue Angels have called Pensacola home since 1954. The team practices over the beach because the open water provides a safe buffer zone and unobstructed sightlines for maneuvers that would be impossible over populated land.

Lt. Cmdr. Brian Vaught, the team's public affairs officer, said the squadron is aware of the parking issues but can't do much about them.

"We're focused on flying safely and putting on a good show," Vaught said. "The logistics on the ground are really a local government matter."

The team flies 30 to 35 practice sessions per year at Pensacola Beach. Each one draws a crowd that would fill a minor league baseball stadium.

The schedule is posted online and widely shared. Websites track the team's movements. Facebook groups alert members when the jets are warming up. By the time the first F/A-18 lifts off from Sherman Field at Naval Air Station Pensacola, thousands of people are already in position.

No easy fix

Back on Ariola Drive, Linda Odom has developed her own system. She runs her errands early on Wednesdays. She parks in her garage instead of the driveway. She keeps the phone number for the county's non-emergency line saved in her favorites.

"I'm not going to stop loving the Blue Angels," she said. "My dad was a Navy pilot. I grew up watching them. But something has to give."

She gestured toward Via de Luna, where a line of cars crept eastward looking for any open spot.

"It used to be locals and a few tourists. Now it's everybody. The whole Gulf Coast."

Above her, six blue and gold jets traced a perfect diamond across the cloudless sky. The roar shook windows for miles. On the beach, thousands of people tilted their heads back and watched.

The minivan with Alabama plates was still in her driveway when she got home.
